Neonatal Geoffroy's tamarins emerge weighing approximately 46.03 grams [Wwb = approximately 46.03 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the typical altricial state of newborn callitrichids. These neonates are entirely dependent on their mothers and other group members for thermoregulation and transport. Within the first weeks of life, the developing infant clings to the fur of its caregivers, nursing frequently. The transition to nutritional independence is a gradual process, but the period from birth to weaning is typically complete by 56 days after birth [tx = 56 days after birth] under standard captive conditions at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This relatively rapid weaning timeframe is characteristic of the genus and allows females to resume cycling and potentially produce two litters per year. The energetic cost of lactation during this pre-weaning phase is substantial, and the female's body condition is a critical determinant of litter survival. By the time weaning concludes, the juvenile tamarin has usually achieved a body mass of 225 grams [Wwx = 225 grams], representing a more than fourfold increase from its birth weight and signaling a successful transition to solid foods.

Reproduction in Geoffroy's tamarin is characterized by a pattern of twinning, with females most commonly delivering two offspring per parturition. The gestation period for this species lasts 142 days [tg = 142 days] when the female is maintained at a core body temperature of 36.0 °C [T = 36.0 °C], a duration that is consistent with that of other members of the Saguinus genus. Following parturition, the female is capable of producing a maximum of approximately two litters per year [F_R_i = approximately two litters per year] under optimal captive conditions, with each litter typically containing one offspring [N_R_i = each litter typically containing one offspring]. The potential for such a high reproductive rate is facilitated by the cooperative breeding system typical of callitrichids, in which fathers and older siblings assist in carrying and provisioning the infants. This alloparental care reduces the energetic burden on the lactating female, allowing her to recover more quickly and conceive sooner than would be possible with exclusive maternal care. The timing of these reproductive events is tightly linked to the social dynamics and nutritional status of the group.

As juveniles mature, the onset of puberty marks a significant physiological transition. Under standard laboratory conditions, individuals reach puberty at 548 days after birth [tp = 548 days after birth] when housed at a stable thermal environment of 36.0 °C [T = 36.0 °C]. This delayed sexual maturation, relative to the weaning age, allows ample time for the development of social skills, foraging competence, and the attainment of adult body size. The ultimate adult body mass for this species is approximately 499.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 499.3 grams], a value typical for a medium-bodied callitrichid. This asymptotic mass is not usually achieved until well after puberty, as individuals continue to grow and deposit fat reserves. The interplay between growth and reproduction is finely tuned; early maturation could compromise eventual adult size and health, while excessive delay reduces lifetime reproductive output. Consequently, the timing of puberty represents an evolutionary compromise that balances these competing pressures.

Longevity in Geoffroy's tamarin has been documented in both field and captive settings. The maximum recorded lifespan for the species is 20.5 years [am = 20.5 years] when individuals are maintained at a core temperature of 36.0 °C [T = 36.0 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, compared to other mammals of a similar body mass, is a hallmark of the primate order and reflects a slow life-history strategy. During these later years, females may experience reproductive senescence, though many individuals remain reproductively viable well into their second decade. The physiological mechanisms underlying this longevity include efficient DNA repair, slow cellular turnover, and a robust immune system, traits that are likely conserved across the Platyrrhini. In the wild, however, extrinsic mortality factors such as predation and disease typically reduce realized lifespan far below this captive maximum, illustrating the profound impact of environmental context on life-history expression.

The energetic demands of this life-history profile are substantial, and the species' metabolic rate provides a key physiological underpinning for its pattern of growth and reproduction. Basal metabolic rate in Geoffroy's tamarin, measured as maximal resting oxygen consumption at a thermoneutral temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], reaches 234.4 milliliters per hour [JOi = 234.4 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic intensity is necessary to support the high costs of gestation, lactation, and the active, arboreal lifestyle typical of the genus. Interestingly, this value is slightly elevated compared to predictions based on body mass alone for Neotropical primates, potentially reflecting the species' small body size and high surface-area-to-volume ratio, which increases thermoregulatory demands. The ability to sustain this elevated metabolism is contingent upon a diet rich in fruit, nectar, and small prey items, resources that require considerable cognitive and locomotory effort to harvest. Consequently, the metabolic phenotype of this species is intimately linked to its ecological niche as a frugivorous and insectivorous canopy forager.
